lessons.title: Accord des adjectifs
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Adjective agreement: Adjectives agree with the noun they describe: un libro rojo, unas mochilas rojas.
lessons.objective: Accordez les adjectifs au genre et au nombre du nom : un sac rouge, des sacs rouges, une petite trousse, des petites trousses.
lessons.foundationTie: Reuses the articles, nouns and present-tense descriptions from Foundation, and the regular verbs introduced in Core 1–3.
lessons.focus: Gender and number agreement for common descriptive adjectives

grammar.explanation: In French, an adjective generally agrees with the noun it describes in gender and number. For many adjectives, add -e for feminine and -s for plural: petit, petite, petits, petites. Rouge already ends in -e, so masculine and feminine singular look alike; the plural is rouges. French adjectives often follow the noun (un sac rouge), though common adjectives such as petit usually precede it (un petit cahier). Spoken final -s is normally silent.
grammar.caution: The article also changes with the noun: un sac, une trousse, des sacs. Not every adjective forms its feminine simply by adding -e.

lessons.scene: Dans une papeterie, une cliente demande un sac à dos rouge et compare plusieurs cahiers.
dialogue: Bonjour, je cherche un sac à dos rouge.|Hello, I'm looking for a red backpack.
Les sacs à dos rouges sont ici.|The red backpacks are here.
Et ce petit cahier bleu ?|And this small blue notebook?
Il est petit, mais les livres sont intéressants.|It is small, but the books are interesting.
La vendeuse est gentille.|The sales assistant is kind.
Je voudrais deux petits cahiers, s'il vous plaît.|I would like two small notebooks, please.
lessons.speaking: Role-play a stationery-shop visit. Ask the sales assistant for a red backpack and two small notebooks. Describe one item with a singular adjective and several items with plural adjectives. Ask where the red backpacks are, answer a related question, and confirm the choice. Use English only to explain a word if requested.

lessons.title: Mon, ton et son
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Mi, tu and su: Possessives agree with what is possessed, not the owner: mi libro, mis libros; tu mesa, tus mesas.
lessons.objective: Choisissez mon, ton ou son selon le genre et le nombre de l'objet possédé, et non selon le propriétaire : mon cahier, ma table, mes livres.
lessons.foundationTie: Reuses school and classroom nouns plus articles from Foundation; builds on Core 4's gender and number agreement.

grammar.explanation: A French possessive determiner agrees with the thing possessed. Say mon cahier but ma table, and mes livres in the plural. The owner may be male or female: son téléphone can mean his phone or her phone; context tells you whose it is. Before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel or mute h, use mon, ton or son for pronunciation: mon amie.

model.first_singular: mon cahier / ma table / mes livres
model.second_singular: ton cahier / ta table / tes crayons
model.third_singular: son téléphone / sa table / ses livres

grammar.caution: Son does not by itself reveal whether the owner is a man or a woman. A person's name or sentence context resolves that ambiguity.

lessons.scene: Après le cours, deux camarades cherchent leurs affaires; la professeure cherche aussi son téléphone.
dialogue: Mon sac à dos est dans la salle de classe.|My backpack is in the classroom.
Mes livres sont dans mon sac à dos.|My books are in my backpack.
Où est ton cahier ?|Where is your notebook?
Tes crayons sont ici, sur la table.|Your pencils are here, on the table.
La professeure cherche son téléphone.|The teacher is looking for her phone.
Le téléphone de la professeure est sur la table.|The teacher's phone is on the table.
lessons.speaking: Role-play finding things after class. Ask a classmate where their notebook is, tell them their pencils are here, and say where your backpack and books are. Explain that the teacher is looking for her phone and identify where it is. Use mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes and son/sa/ses in context.

lessons.title: Avoir : possessions et besoins
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Tener: possessions and needs: Tener is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.
lessons.objective: Utilisez avoir au présent pour exprimer ce que l'on possède et certains besoins : j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, ils ont ; j'ai faim, elle a soif.
lessons.foundationTie: Reuses classroom and food vocabulary from Foundation and possessives from Core 5; introduces an irregular present-tense verb.
lessons.focus: Present-tense avoir, possession, hunger and thirst

grammar.explanation: Avoir is irregular: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. French uses avoir where English uses be for hunger and thirst: j'ai faim (I am hungry), elle a soif (she is thirsty). For possession, use j'ai un livre or nous avons de l'eau. Je shortens to j' before ai.
grammar.caution: Do not translate 'I am hungry' as je suis faim. Say j'ai faim. Avoir can also appear in other fixed expressions learned later.

lessons.scene: Après un cours, des amis vérifient ce qu'ils ont à manger et à boire avant le déjeuner.
dialogue: J'ai faim après le cours.|I am hungry after class.
Nous avons de l'eau dans le sac à dos.|We have water in the backpack.
Luis a deux sandwichs.|Luis has two sandwiches.
Mes amis ont le temps de manger.|My friends have time to eat.
Tu as un verre pour Ana ?|Do you have a glass for Ana?
lessons.speaking: Role-play planning a snack after class. Say that you are hungry, ask whether your partner has water or a glass, and report what Ana, Luis and your friends have. Use j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons and ils/elles ont, then confirm what the group still needs.

words.note: Cours is a class session; salle de classe is the classroom.
